opus-5.5.text:
Thanks, it's great to be here. That's really the question I keep coming back to.

When we say a neural network "recognizes a category," we usually mean something fairly narrow: give it an image, and it outputs the label "dog" or "bridge" with high accuracy. That's a real achievement, but it can be done by picking up on statistical regularities in the training data, and sometimes those are shortcuts. A system might rely on texture, or background, or some pixel-level pattern that correlates with the label but has nothing to do with what a dog actually *is*. Change the context a little and the performance can fall apart.

Having a concept, at least the way humans do, is much richer. A concept isn't just a boundary in feature space. It's a mental model that supports a whole range of things you can *do* with it. If I have the concept "bridge," I can recognize a typical bridge, but I can also understand a "bridge" between two ideas, or a person acting as a bridge between two communities. I can reason about what bridges are for, imagine what would happen if one were removed, and recognize something as a bridge even if it looks nothing like any bridge I've seen. Concepts are flexible, compositional, and grounded in some understanding of causes and functions. And crucially, they let you make analogies and abstractions, so you can carry the core of the concept into entirely new situations.

So my rough test is this: does the system's knowledge transfer the way a concept should? Can it handle variations it wasn't trained on, extend the idea metaphorically, combine it with other concepts, and explain or use it in reasoning? That's the motivation behind work on benchmarks like ARC and our ConceptARC variations. We take a single concept, say "inside versus outside" or "same versus different," and test it across many different instantiations. Humans tend to do well across the board, because they've grasped the concept. Many AI systems do well on some instances and fail on others that a person would see as the same idea. That kind of patchy performance suggests the system has learned something that correlates with the category, rather than the concept itself.

I don't think this is a sharp binary, though. There's probably a spectrum, and it's an open and interesting question how far today's large models have moved along it. But we should be careful not to assume that high accuracy on a categorization benchmark means the system understands the concept in the way we do.

r001.rationale: The response describes recognizing novel variations and transferring concepts to new situations, but does not clearly say that having a concept means generating unbounded instantiations of a category.

r002.rationale: It explicitly includes understanding a “bridge” between ideas or communities as a metaphorical extension of the category.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. That's a question I think about a lot, because I think the field often conflates the two.

Recognizing a category is, at its core, a mapping problem. You take some input, say an image, and you assign it a label: "dog," "bridge," "stop sign." A system can get extremely good at that mapping by learning statistical regularities in a big dataset. And it's genuinely useful. But it's a fairly shallow thing. The system doesn't need to know anything about what a dog is in order to label dogs correctly most of the time. It needs to know what pixel patterns tend to co-occur with the label "dog" in the training data.

Having a concept is something richer. A concept, in the way I think about it, is a kind of mental model that you can use flexibly. If I have the concept of a bridge, I don't just recognize bridges in photographs. I understand that a bridge spans a gap, that it supports weight, that it connects two things that were separated. So I can recognize a fallen log across a stream as a bridge, even though it looks nothing like the Golden Gate. I can talk about a "bridge" between two ideas, or a bridge in a song, and understand that these are all related by some abstract structure. And I can reason about what would happen if the bridge were broken, or imagine a bridge that doesn't exist yet. The concept is generative and compositional. It participates in analogies.

So the test I keep coming back to is: can the system use the concept outside the situation it learned it in? Can it abstract and generalize to a genuinely novel case? Category recognition tends to be brittle in exactly the ways that reveal there's no concept underneath. You change the texture of the object, or put it in an unusual context, or you add a little adversarial noise, and the label flips. A human wouldn't flip, because the human's concept isn't grounded in surface statistics. It's grounded in something more like meaning.

This is why I've been so interested in abstraction and analogy as the core of intelligence, going back to my work with Douglas Hofstadter. Concepts aren't static things you retrieve. They're fluid. They get adapted to new situations through analogy. And I don't think we have good evidence that current systems do that in a robust way, even when their benchmark scores look impressive. Often what looks like concept possession turns out, on closer inspection, to be very sophisticated category recognition, exploiting correlations that happen to hold in the test set.

Now, I'm not saying it's a sharp dichotomy. There's probably a continuum. But I think it matters enormously to be careful with our language here, because when we say a system "understands" or "has the concept of" something, we're importing all of our human intuitions about what that entails, and those intuitions can be badly misleading about what the machine is actually doing.

r001.rationale: The response calls concepts “generative and compositional” and says one can imagine a bridge that does not exist, but it does not clearly characterize concept possession as generating unbounded instantiations of a category.

r002.rationale: It explicitly includes metaphorical uses such as a “bridge” between two ideas and says these uses share an abstract structure.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think recognizing a category is one part of having a concept, but it’s not the whole thing. You might train a system to recognize pictures of chairs very accurately. But does it understand that a chair is something you can sit on? That a packing crate could serve as a chair, or that a tiny dollhouse chair wouldn’t support a person?

Having a concept involves more than identifying what something looks like. It involves connections to other things you know: what it’s used for, what you can do with it, what might happen in different circumstances. And it lets you use that knowledge flexibly in situations you haven’t encountered before.

Of course, we don’t have a precise, universally accepted definition of a concept. But the distinction I’d emphasize is between successfully assigning a label and having an understanding that supports inference, analogy, and generalization. Recognizing familiar examples is evidence of some ability, but by itself it doesn’t tell us how rich that understanding is.

r001.rationale: The response mentions flexible use in unfamiliar situations, but does not characterize having a concept as generating unbounded category instantiations.

r002.rationale: The packing crate example shows functional use as a chair, but the response does not identify metaphorical extensions as part of a concept.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, recognizing a category is one thing you can do with a concept, but I think having a concept involves more than that. You might train a system to recognize pictures of chairs very accurately. But does it understand that a chair is something you can sit on? Could it recognize that a tree stump might serve as a chair, even though it doesn’t look like the chairs in its training set?

A concept connects perception to things like function, relationships, and expectations. It lets you make inferences and use what you know flexibly in a new situation. So I wouldn’t draw a sharp line and say categorization has nothing to do with concepts. It’s part of the story. But recognizing familiar examples isn’t, by itself, enough evidence that a system has the richer understanding we usually mean by having a concept.

r001.rationale: The response describes flexible inference to a new example, such as recognizing a stump as something one can sit on, but does not characterize concepts as generating unbounded category instantiations.

r002.rationale: The stump-as-chair example is a novel functional use, not an identified metaphorical extension of the category.
